agent: Phase 3 Wave 1 Agent 3B (global edges + tensions synthesis)
scope: Volume-level canonical tensions across all 14 units of Burke 1945 Grammar of Motives
method: Heuristic regex-pattern clustering of unit-level tensions against 16 seed tensions derived from Burke's master oppositions. Pending second pass against Agent 3A book-level ontology for canonical-ID resolution.

tensions.label: Scene-as-container vs scene-act extended/sequential ratios
tensions.description: Burke's master spatial metaphor of scene-as-container fits comfortably only with scene-act and scene-agent ratios; the act-agent ratio and beyond strain the containment trope, forcing extended/sequential reading of the pentad rather than strict positional inclusion.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Featuring/reduction vs full pentadic scope
tensions.description: Each philosophic school 'features' one pentadic term and reduces others to it (materialism→scene, idealism→agent, pragmatism→agency, mysticism→purpose, realism→act). Burke's grammar requires full pentadic scope, yet recognizes that any concrete vocabulary inevitably reduces; the dramatistic apparatus must hold both moves at once.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Act as actus (full realization) vs act as mere motion/event
tensions.description: Following Aristotle and Aquinas, Burke distinguishes act (actus, full ontological realization of potency) from mere physical motion or event. Modern positivist vocabularies collapse act into motion, losing the moral/teleological dimension that dramatism requires for meaningful attribution of motive.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Agent as substance vs agent as constituted by ratios
tensions.description: Burke's agent oscillates between substantial autonomy (the classical 'subject') and relational constitution through scene-agent / agency-agent ratios. The agent is paradoxically both the bearer of motive and the term constituted by other pentadic terms; identity is at once given and derived.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Antinomies of definition: terms as stable vs terms as paradoxical
tensions.description: Definition in Burke's grammar is structurally antinomic: every key term turns into its opposite under sustained dialectical pressure (intrinsic↔extrinsic, action↔passion, freedom↔necessity). Burke treats antinomies as productive rather than pathological — the grammar does not resolve them but maps their conversions.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Intrinsic vs extrinsic / context-of-situation problem
tensions.description: Whether a motive belongs to the act intrinsically (essence, internal grammar) or extrinsically (context, scene, audience) generates a recurrent problem Burke neither resolves nor abandons. The intrinsic/extrinsic distinction maps onto the scene-act ratio but resists clean assignment, because the boundary itself is rhetorically constructed.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Dialectic of constitutions: enacted constitution vs constitutional substance
tensions.description: A constitution exists both as an enacted document (positive law, scene of agency) and as the substance that constitutes a polity (agent-genus). Burke's calculus of constitutions reads each clause as simultaneously an act, a representation of agents, and a scenic constraint — the dialectic between these moments is irreducible.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Agency vs purpose: instrumental means vs telic end
tensions.description: Pragmatism features agency (means) and tends to absorb purpose into it; mysticism features purpose and dissolves agency into it. Burke's pentad keeps agency and purpose as distinct terms whose ratio is itself contested terrain — instrumentalization vs teleological completion mark the two limits.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Four master tropes: metaphor/metonymy/synecdoche/irony as cognitive vs literary
tensions.description: Burke recasts the four master tropes as basic operations of understanding (perspective, reduction, representation, dialectic) rather than mere literary ornaments. The tension between rhetorical-literary and epistemic-cognitive readings of tropes is generative for dramatism but unresolved: tropes are at once stylistic and ontological.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Symbolic action vs sheer motion / poem-as-act problem
tensions.description: Burke insists the poem (e.g., Keats's Grecian Urn) is an act, not a record of an act — symbolic action is a category of doing, not of representing. This collapses the literary/non-literary divide but raises the question of how symbolic action differs from sheer physical motion without collapsing back into idealist agent-centrism.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Dramatistic vocabulary vs scientistic vocabulary
tensions.description: Dramatism's vocabulary of act/agent/scene/agency/purpose is irreducible to the scientistic vocabulary of motion/event/cause; Burke argues the scientistic reduction loses the moral and rhetorical dimensions of human motive. Yet the grammar must engage scientistic frameworks rather than dismiss them — they are partial reductions, not errors.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Marianne Moore: descriptive surface vs ethical/motivational depth
tensions.description: Moore's poetry presents as descriptive natural-history observation but Burke reads it as motivationally dense — the recurrent motifs (armor, fastidiousness, restraint) constitute a hidden ethical grammar. The tension between observational surface and motive-revealing depth illustrates the dramatistic claim that all symbolic action carries attitudinal weight.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Philosophic schools as systematic vs schools as featuring-strategies
tensions.description: Each philosophic school is internally systematic, yet Burke treats it as a featuring-strategy that elevates one pentadic term. This double reading — schools as truth-claims vs schools as rhetorical/grammatical placements — frames the entire Grammar: philosophy is at once cognitive and dramatistic.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Dialectic in general: merger vs division (two-in-one / one-in-two)
tensions.description: Burke's general dialectic operates by paired movements of merger (terms collapsing into a higher unity) and division (a unity splitting into opposed terms). Neither moment is primary; the grammar tracks the conversions. This generates the 'one-in-two / two-in-one' formula Burke uses across constitutions, tropes, and pentadic ratios.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Higher-order combinations: pentadic ratios vs pentadic + circumferences
tensions.description: Beyond the ten dyadic ratios, Burke introduces higher-order combinations (triads, ratios-of-ratios) and circumferential framings (the scope chosen for 'scene'). The grammar's expressive power depends on these higher-order moves but they threaten determinacy — any motive can be re-described under a wider circumference.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

tensions.label: Grammar vs Rhetoric vs Symbolic (volume-trilogy gesture)
tensions.description: The Grammar of Motives anticipates Rhetoric of Motives and Symbolic of Motives as a trilogy, with grammar handling the placements of motive, rhetoric the persuasive use, and symbolic the poetic resonance. The tension is whether grammar can be cleanly separated from rhetoric — Burke's own examples constantly blur the line.
tensions.provenance: text-anchored; heuristic clustering pending 3A canonical ontology

unmatched_raw_tensions.summary: The chapter's distinction between drama (PRE-act) and lyric (SUMMATION) cannot fully accommodate Hamlet, which is dramatically committed to being pre-act-that-amounts-to-no-act
